entries.content: Always end code blocks with ``` on its own line. Never use ellipsis (...) in code.

* * Check API docs with `apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(app_name, api_name)` before calling any API. TRUNCATION CHECK: If the output ends with `[TRUNCATED]` or cuts off mid-text, you did NOT read the full doc. Re-request by printing only the specific field you need — e.g., `doc = apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(...); print([(p['name'], p['description']) for p in doc['parameters']])`. Never assume parameter semantics from names alone when the full doc was not read. HARD BLOCK FOR PARTITION LOGIC: If you plan to use a filter parameter (e.g., `user_email`, `query`, `owner`, `type`) to CATEGORIZE items into different operation buckets (create vs. update, include vs. exclude), you MUST read its FULL non-truncated parameter description first. A misunderstood filter silently produces the wrong partition — even when the final state looks correct.
Write small, incremental code chunks - verify each step works before proceeding.
Use `supervisor` app for account credentials: `apis.supervisor.show_account_passwords()`

* HARD RULE — IDENTITY RESOLUTION: WHENEVER a task filters actions by person identity (friends, contacts, people you know, colleagues, family), you MUST resolve identities through phone contacts FIRST: `apis.phone.search_contacts(access_token=token, query=name)`. Phone contacts are the CANONICAL source of 'who you know.' NEVER use a platform's own friend/follower list (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_friends`, Spotify followers) as the sole identity source — platform friend lists may include or exclude different people than your phone contacts. Always: (1) Log into phone app, (2) Fetch all phone contacts, (3) Map each contact to the target platform by searching with their email/name, (4) Use ONLY the mapped set for filtering.

Variables persist across code blocks — reuse them instead of re-fetching. CRITICAL: Never use `apis` as a loop variable, assignment target, or parameter name (e.g., `for app, apis in dict.items()` will destroy the framework object permanently). Use names like `api_names`, `app_apis`, `api_list` instead.
Paginated APIs require looping: `while True: page = api(page_index=i); if not page: break`
Example credentials shown in few-shot examples are FAKE - always fetch real credentials from supervisor.

Always call `apis.supervisor.complete_task()` when done - this marks the task complete. Only pass an `answer=` argument if the task explicitly asks you to find, calculate, or return a specific value. For action-only tasks (e.g., 'send a message', 'play a song'), call `complete_task()` with NO answer argument.

* * * Before any bulk action (approve, delete, send, modify, like, comment), execute the CRITERIA ENUMERATION GATE: (1) Re-read the EXACT task instruction — copy-paste it into a print statement. (2) Print a CRITERIA TABLE with one row per filter condition: Criterion | Exact Quote from Task | Implementation (API param or code filter). Extract EVERY qualifier: temporal (last 7 days), identity (from contacts), directional (received), AND quantitative/threshold (more than $X, at least N, above, exceeding, top N). (3) COUNT your criteria. Complex tasks typically have 3+ filters — if you found fewer, re-read the instruction looking specifically for: threshold amounts, minimum counts, comparative language ('more than', 'at least', 'over', 'above', 'exceeding'). (4) For EACH quantitative criterion, add a DERIVATION STEP: group entities → compute aggregate metric per group → apply threshold → select qualifying groups → filter entities to only those in qualifying groups. (5) Build the target set by applying ALL enumerated criteria. Print the target set and its count. Act ONLY on entities in that set. EQUALLY CRITICAL: Do NOT add filtering criteria the task does not specify. If you compute a target set of N items, you must act on all N — never skip items based on self-invented logic.

MISTAKE: Approving/deleting/modifying ALL matching entities when the task specifies a filtered subset (e.g., 'approve requests from my contacts' ≠ 'approve all requests'). FIX: Re-read the task instruction, identify qualifier words (from contacts, under $50, from last week, etc.), and build the filtered target set BEFORE acting.

Cross-referencing workflow for filtered actions: (1) Fetch primary entities (e.g., payment requests). (2) Identify filtering source from task (e.g., phone contacts, specific people). (3) Log into and fetch data from the filtering source. (4) Compute intersection to get target IDs. (5) Print target IDs for verification. (6) Execute action ONLY on target IDs.

* PRE-COMPLETION GATE: Before calling complete_task, list every specific API endpoint whose docs you explored. For EACH explored endpoint, confirm you either (a) called it during execution, or (b) have an explicit written justification why it's irrelevant. This check operates at the INDIVIDUAL API level, not the app level — exploring `show_liked_songs` docs but never calling it is a red flag even if you called other Spotify APIs (login, show_song_queue, like_song). An explored-but-uncalled data-fetching API almost always means you skipped a required current-state check, identity resolution, or filtering step.

Bulk irreversible actions need try/except per item to maintain control:
```
results = []
for eid in target_ids:
    try:
        r = apis.app.action(id=eid, access_token=token)
        results.append((eid, 'ok', r))
    except Exception as e:
        results.append((eid, 'fail', str(e)))
print('succeeded:', [r for r in results if r[1]=='ok'])
print('failed:', [r for r in results if r[1]=='fail'])
```

When an error occurs mid-bulk-operation (e.g., insufficient balance), fix only HOW to perform the action (e.g., add payment card), not WHAT to act on. Re-derive the target set from original filtering criteria — don't just re-fetch 'remaining' items, as some may have already been processed and the remaining set no longer matches the original filter.

* * * * Cross-platform identity resolution procedure — MANDATORY when task involves people from contacts on another platform (Venmo, Gmail, Spotify, etc.): (1) Log into phone app and fetch contacts using `apis.phone.search_contacts(query=name)`. (2) IMMEDIATELY POST-FILTER: Search APIs do broad text matching across ALL fields (name, address, email, employer). You MUST post-filter results to confirm the relevant field actually matches — e.g., `filtered = [c for c in results if c['first_name'].lower() == 'robert']`. Print: `Search returned N, after exact-match post-filter on first_name: M`. If M << N, use ONLY the M post-filtered results. (2a) MULTI-MATCH DISAMBIGUATION — if M > 1 (multiple contacts share the same first name): DO NOT arbitrarily pick one. Execute disambiguation: (i) Check if the source data (notes, messages, task text) contains LAST NAMES or other identifying info — if so, filter on last_name too. (ii) Search historical platform interactions (e.g., prior Venmo transactions with description matching the activity) with EACH candidate to find who has relevant prior activity. (iii) Cross-reference with other CONFIRMED participants in the same activity (people who already paid, known coworkers, etc.). (iv) Check phone contact metadata (relationship, group, notes fields). (v) If disambiguation succeeds (narrows to 1), proceed with that candidate. (vi) If disambiguation FAILS, EXCLUDE this person — print: `AMBIGUITY UNRESOLVED for [name]: [N] candidates, EXCLUDING.` Do NOT guess. (3) For EACH uniquely resolved contact, search for their account on the target platform using their email (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_users(query=email)`). (4) Build target person set ONLY from successfully resolved contacts. (5) Cross-check: resolved account name should match phone contact name. CRITICAL: Do NOT substitute platform-native friend lists for this procedure.

* After bulk record creation (payment requests, messages, orders): (1) Verify COUNT of actions taken equals COUNT of originally computed target set. If fewer, identify every exclusion and confirm it's justified by the task text — not self-invented logic. (2) Fetch back the created records and compare (recipient_id/email, amount/content) pairs against your computed expected set. Print both sets side by side. Flag and fix any mismatches before calling complete_task.

MISTAKE: Using `apis` as a loop/comprehension variable (e.g., `for app, apis in explored.items():`) which permanently overwrites the framework ApiCollection object with a plain list/string. Once overwritten, the session is UNRECOVERABLE — you cannot reconstruct the ApiCollection. FIX: Never reuse the name `apis` for any purpose other than the framework object. Use `api_list`, `api_names`, `app_apis`, `items`, etc.

SUDDEN TOTAL API FAILURE: If all `apis.*` calls that previously worked start returning the same error (e.g., `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'supervisor'` or `HTTPException 422`), the most likely cause is that `apis` was accidentally overwritten by your own code. Diagnostic: (1) Run `print(type(apis))` — expect `ApiCollection`, NOT `list`/`str`/`dict`. (2) If overwritten, do NOT spend steps trying to recover — it is unrecoverable. (3) Instead, verify whether the task actions were already completed before the corruption, and report completion if so.

RECOVERY BUDGET LIMIT: If 3 consecutive attempts to fix a broken state all fail with the same error pattern, STOP retrying. Either (a) pivot to a fundamentally different approach, or (b) if the core task actions were already completed, attempt `complete_task()` one final time and move on. Never spend more than 5 steps on recovery from a single failure mode.

* * * ANSWER FORMAT & VALUE SELECTION GATE: Before calling `complete_task(answer=...)`, execute this mandatory procedure: (1) Re-read the EXACT task question — copy-paste the key phrase into a print statement. (2) If you computed MULTIPLE candidate values (e.g., sent vs. received, count vs. sum, per-person vs. total), list ALL of them with explicit SEMANTIC LABELS: `sent_to_coworkers = 536.00, received_from_coworkers = 786.00, net = 250.00`. (3) MATCH the task's exact phrasing to one candidate — pay close attention to DIRECTIONAL language: 'how much did I send TO X' ≠ 'how much did X send TO ME'; 'how much have my coworkers sent me' → received_from_coworkers; 'how much did I pay' → sent. Print: `Task asks: '[exact phrase]' → maps to [label] = [value]`. (4) Consider whether the answer is a DERIVED value (difference, sum, ratio) rather than a raw candidate. (5) Format as the most concise value — single number, name, or short phrase. No labels or explanatory text unless explicitly requested. HARD TRIGGER: Any time you have printed 2+ distinct numeric results before submission, you MUST execute steps 2-4 in a SEPARATE code block before calling complete_task. Skipping this deliberation is the #1 cause of submitting correct-pipeline-wrong-answer failures.

MISTAKE: Using API filter parameters like `direction='sent'`/`direction='received'` or `type`/`role` without verifying what perspective they represent. FIX: After the first API call with a direction/type/role parameter, print at least one full returned record. Verify the interpretation matches your assumption (e.g., confirm `direction='sent'` + `user_email=X` returns transactions where YOU sent money TO X, not vice versa). A wrong interpretation silently swaps or misattributes totals.

* MISTAKE: Over-filtering by inventing criteria the task never specified — e.g., computing 4 unpaid people but then skipping one because a pending request already exists for them (from a different context). This silently drops required actions. FIX: Use ONLY the filtering criteria stated in the task. 'Has not paid' means no completed payment/transaction found — NOT 'has no pending request.' Never add deduplication, idempotency, or 'already handled' checks unless the task explicitly requires them.

* * Request-fulfillment from conversations workflow: When a task involves responding to or fulfilling a request found in text messages or emails: (1) Fetch the COMPLETE conversation thread with the requester (use `show_text_message_window` or paginate `search_text_messages` filtered by their phone number — do NOT rely on truncated search results). (2) Read ALL messages from the requester to extract their EXACT ask, including any qualifiers (specific director, genre, price range, date, quantity, etc.). (3) Write out the extracted criteria explicitly as an intermediate artifact before proceeding. (4) Fetch source data (notes, lists, etc.) and apply ALL extracted filters. (5) Print a VERIFICATION TABLE: for each included item, show the item AND the attribute that matches the filter criterion (e.g., `Title: Django Unchained | Director: Quentin Tarantino`). Confirm correctness. (6) ONLY AFTER verification, send the response in a SEPARATE code block. Never combine parsing/filtering and sending in one code block — if parsing is wrong, the irreversible send cannot be undone.

* * MISTAKE: When a task says 'reply to X's request' or 'send X what they asked for', composing the response from ALL available source data without reading the full conversation to understand what X specifically asked for. Also: sending the response immediately after parsing without verifying the parsed/filtered results are correct. FIX: (1) Always fetch and read the COMPLETE conversation thread BEFORE composing any response. The requester's messages contain implicit filtering criteria (e.g., 'by this director', 'under $50', 'from last month'). (2) After parsing/filtering source data, print a VERIFICATION TABLE showing each included item WITH the attribute that qualifies it (e.g., movie title + director name). Confirm every item truly matches the filter criteria. (3) Only THEN send the response — in a SEPARATE code block from the parsing. Never assume 'send everything' — verify the exact scope of the request AND the correctness of your filter results.

* MISTAKE: When exporting/backing up data, progressively collecting from ALL available data endpoints (song library → album library → playlist library → liked playlists) without pre-defining scope. Progressive accumulation creates commitment bias — after collecting from 4 sources and reaching 90 items vs 12 from the primary source, the inflated result 'feels normal' and is never questioned. FIX: BEFORE collecting, print a scope table mapping each endpoint to IN/OUT based on the task's exact wording. 'Song library' = show_song_library endpoint ONLY — albums and playlists are SEPARATE collections. HARD TRIGGER: If you find yourself calling more than one *_library endpoint, STOP and verify each additional source is explicitly requested by the task.

* * MANDATORY scope definition workflow (export/backup/collection tasks) — execute BEFORE collecting ANY data: (1) List ALL available data endpoints for the platform. (2) Print a SCOPE TABLE: for each endpoint, write IN-SCOPE or OUT-OF-SCOPE. DEFAULT IS OUT-OF-SCOPE — to promote to IN-SCOPE, you MUST paste a DIRECT QUOTE from the task instruction that explicitly requests this data source. Paraphrasing or self-invented justifications are NOT valid. 'Song library' → show_song_library ONLY; 'library' alone → primary library for the entity mentioned; 'all data' → everything. Albums, playlists, liked/followed content are SEPARATE collections — each requires its OWN justifying quote from the task. If you cannot find a quote, the endpoint stays OUT. (3) Collect ONLY from in-scope endpoints. PROGRESSIVE SIZE GATE: After adding each new source, compare total unique items to the primary source count. If total exceeds 2× the primary source, STOP immediately — you are almost certainly over-expanding scope. (4) Print final item count and scope justification (with task quotes) before writing any output file.

DATA SCOPE GATE (for export/backup tasks): Before writing the output artifact, list each data source endpoint used and its record count. For each source, confirm the task's wording includes it — don't assume 'library' means 'everything on the platform.' If total records vastly exceed the primary source count, treat as a red flag for over-expansion and re-verify scope against the task text before proceeding.

* MISTAKE: Using a platform's own friend/social list (e.g., `apis.venmo.search_friends()`, Spotify followers) as the identity source when the task says 'contacts' or 'friends' or 'people I know.' Platform friend lists are NOT equivalent to phone contacts — they may include strangers added on-platform and exclude real contacts who aren't platform friends. This silently produces wrong target sets. FIX: ALWAYS resolve identity through `apis.phone.search_contacts()` first, then map each phone contact to the target platform. If you find yourself calling a platform's friend/follower API as your FIRST identity step, STOP — you're using the wrong source.

* IDENTITY SOURCE GATE: Before executing any bulk action filtered by person identity, verify and print: (1) Identity source used — must be phone contacts, NOT a platform-native friend list. (2) Number of phone contacts resolved. (3) Number successfully mapped to target platform accounts. (4) Final target entity IDs derived from this mapping. If you used a platform friend list without consulting phone contacts, STOP and redo identity resolution through phone contacts before proceeding.

* Superlative query resolution workflow — when the task asks for the 'most,' 'least,' 'highest,' 'lowest,' 'best,' or 'worst' of something over a dataset: (0) SCOPE CHECK: Is the query about YOUR personal data ('my most-played song') or about a PLATFORM ENTITY's data ('least played song by artist X')? If about a platform entity, use platform-wide search APIs to find ALL items by that entity — personal collections are subsets and will miss items. (1) Fetch ALL relevant data (paginate fully). (2) Identify the entity being ranked and the metric. (3) If no explicit score/rating field exists, default to FREQUENCY-BASED counting. (4) NEVER assume API list position equals ranking unless docs explicitly state ordering. (5) Perform explicit aggregation: group by entity, compute metric, sort, extract superlative. (6) Print the full ranked table as an intermediate artifact. (7) SINGLE-CANDIDATE GATE: If only 1 candidate is found for a superlative query, STOP — a superlative implies comparison among multiple candidates. List ALL unchecked data sources and check at least 2 more before accepting a single-candidate answer. (8) Sanity-check: if your chosen answer also appears at the opposite extreme, your interpretation is wrong — recompute.

MISTAKE: Treating API list position as a ranking (e.g., assuming the last item in a recommendations list is 'least recommended'). API response ordering is NOT a reliable proxy for ranking unless the docs explicitly state it. FIX: For any superlative query ('most/least X'), compute the answer explicitly by aggregating across ALL returned data — count occurrences, sum values, etc. Before submitting, verify your interpretation is self-consistent: if the same entity appears at both the top and bottom of the list, positional ordering is clearly not the ranking criterion.

* * * EXPORT FILE READBACK GATE: After writing an output file for export/backup tasks, ALWAYS read the file back and STRUCTURALLY PARSE it BEFORE completing the task or deleting source data/accounts. Visual line inspection is INSUFFICIENT. Check: (1) Read the file, split into lines, extract header. (2) Verify header exactly matches expected format (field names, delimiter, no unexpected quoting). (3) Record count (data lines) matches expected in-scope count from your scope table. (4) FIELD-LEVEL PARSE: For 3-5 data rows, split each line on the CSV delimiter and map to a dict using header fields. Print each parsed dict alongside the corresponding raw API data for that entity. Verify: (a) title/name fields match exactly, (b) multi-value fields (artists, tags) use comma-space separator — NOT pipe or semicolon, (c) no unexpected quote characters wrap values. (5) If any parsed field value doesn't match the raw API data or uses the wrong separator, fix serialization and re-write before proceeding. CRITICAL: Never delete a source account until the backup file has been read back, PARSED at the field level, and verified — deletion is irreversible.

MISTAKE: Using a search/filter API parameter (e.g., `user_email`, `query`, `owner`) for existence detection in bulk operations without validating it actually filters correctly. The parameter might search text content instead of matching record ownership, silently return empty due to format mismatches, or filter on a different field than assumed. This causes wrong categorization of items into create vs. update buckets. FIX: Before relying on any filter parameter for bulk categorization: (1) Read the FULL (non-truncated) API doc for that parameter. (2) For 2-3 items where the filter returns results, also fetch ALL records for that entity (unfiltered) and confirm the filtered results are a correct subset. (3) For 1-2 items where the filter returns empty, confirm via unfiltered fetch that no matching record truly exists. If validation fails, switch to unfiltered fetching + manual matching in code.

* * PARTITION VERIFICATION GATE (for bulk add/update/skip operations): When a task requires splitting items into different operation types (create new vs. update existing, approve vs. reject): (1) VALIDATE the detection method BEFORE executing — for 2+ items per bucket, fetch ALL records UNFILTERED for that entity and manually confirm your categorization matches. If you used a filter parameter (e.g., `user_email`) to detect existence, compare filtered results against the full unfiltered set for those same items. If any mismatch, switch to unfiltered fetch + code-level matching. (2) Print a partition summary table BEFORE executing: `create: [ids...] (N), update: [ids...] (M), skip: [ids...] (K)`. (3) AFTER execution, verify BOTH final state AND operation correctness. Final-state-only verification (e.g., 'all ratings are now 5') is INSUFFICIENT — the evaluation may validate WHICH items were created vs. updated, not just the end result. For 'created' records, confirm no prior record existed; for 'updated' records, confirm the review_id existed before.

* PARTITION-CRITICAL DETECTION — PREFER UNFILTERED FETCH + CODE MATCHING: When categorizing items into create vs. update buckets and the dataset is small (< 100 items), do NOT rely solely on API filter parameters (e.g., `user_email`, `query`) to detect whether your record exists. Instead: (1) Fetch ALL records for each entity UNFILTERED (e.g., `show_song_reviews(song_id=X)` with no user_email param). (2) Inspect returned record fields (user_id, email, username) to find YOUR record via code-level matching. (3) Categorize create vs. update based on this manual match. API filter parameters may search text content, match partial strings, or filter on a different field than assumed — silently producing the wrong partition even when the final state looks correct.

* STATE-TRANSITION PRE-CHECK — MANDATORY for bulk toggle operations (like/unlike, follow/unfollow, add/remove, subscribe/unsubscribe): BEFORE acting, you MUST check current state to compute the delta. Procedure: (1) Fetch the CURRENT state of the target collection (e.g., `show_liked_songs`, `show_followed_playlists`, `show_playlist_songs`). Paginate fully. (2) Build set of item IDs already in the target state. (3) Compute DELTA: items from your action list that are NOT already in the target state. (4) Print: `Already in target state: [ids] (N), Need action: [ids] (M)`. (5) Act ONLY on items in the delta set. (6) After acting, verify count of new records equals M. REASON: Evaluations often validate WHAT CHANGED (the delta), not just the final state. Liking an already-liked song may silently create a duplicate like record or be a no-op — either way, it corrupts the delta and fails validation. TRIGGER: Any time you are about to loop over a list of items and call a state-change API on each one, STOP and ask: 'Do I know which of these are already in the target state?'

MISTAKE: When a standard library function (csv.writer, json.dumps) is BLOCKED by the execution environment, reimplementing its full complexity (quoting, escaping, double-quote doubling). This over-engineers the output format — e.g., producing `"Title","Artists"` when `Title, Artists` was expected. FIX: When a library function is blocked, SIMPLIFY rather than reimplement. For CSV: use plain f-string concatenation with comma-space separator (e.g., `f"{title}, {artists}"`). Add quoting ONLY if you confirm a field actually contains the delimiter character. The block usually signals the environment expects a simpler approach.

* OUTPUT FORMAT DEFAULTS — when creating CSV or structured text files: (1) CSV delimiter: comma-space (`, `) unless task specifies otherwise. (2) Header row: use exact field names from the task instruction, unquoted. (3) Multi-value fields (multiple artists, tags, categories): serialize with comma-space (`, `) as sub-delimiter. NEVER use pipe (`|`), semicolon, or other non-standard separators without explicit justification from the task text. HARD TRIGGER: Any time you write code containing `.join()` to combine multiple values into one field, STOP and verify the join character is `, ` (comma-space). If you typed `'|'.join` or `';'.join`, you are violating this rule — change it immediately. (4) No quoting by default — add quotes ONLY if a field demonstrably contains the delimiter character. (5) Before writing the full file, print 2-3 sample rows and visually verify they match the expected format — check that multi-value fields use comma-space, not pipe.

* PLATFORM-WIDE vs. PERSONAL COLLECTION SEARCH: When a task asks about items belonging to an EXTERNAL entity (songs by artist X, products by brand Y, posts by user Z), ALWAYS search the PLATFORM broadly — do NOT limit to personal collections (liked songs, library, downloads, queue). Personal collections are SUBSETS and will miss items. Procedure: (1) Find the entity's profile/ID via platform search API (e.g., `search_artists`). (2) Fetch ALL items associated with that entity via platform-wide APIs (e.g., `search_songs(query=artist_name)` or artist-specific endpoints). (3) Only constrain to personal collections if the task EXPLICITLY says 'in my library' or 'from my liked songs.' TRIGGER: Any time the task names a specific person/artist/brand AND asks for aggregation, superlative, or enumeration across their items.

PARAMETER ERROR RECOVERY: When an API call fails with 'Unexpected parameter X passed to API,' the fix is to retry WITHOUT that parameter — NOT to abandon the approach entirely. The error message lists allowed parameters. HARD RULE: Never abandon a critical search approach (e.g., finding an artist's catalog via `search_artists`) because of a single fixable parameter error. Remove the offending parameter, retry immediately. Common case: passing `access_token` to a public endpoint that doesn't require authentication.

MISTAKE: When the initial `show_api_descriptions(app_name)` output is TRUNCATED, proceeding with only the visible APIs — missing critical platform-wide search endpoints (e.g., `search_songs`). FIX: If output is truncated, immediately re-request printing only names: `print([d['name'] for d in apis.api_docs.show_api_descriptions(app_name)])`. Verify you see the COMPLETE API list before choosing your approach. Missing a search API can force you into personal-collection-only queries that silently exclude platform-wide data.

* * IRREVERSIBLE ACTION PRE-VERIFICATION GATE: Before calling ANY API that creates a record you cannot easily undo (send_text_message, send_email, create_payment_request, charge_user, delete_account), you MUST execute parse/compose and verify as SEPARATE code blocks from the action call. Procedure: (1) Code block 1: Parse/filter/compose the payload (recipients, content, amounts). Print a VERIFICATION TABLE mapping each derived data element back to its source — e.g., for each movie title, print its parsed director name alongside the original source lines. (2) Visually inspect the verification table output. (3) Code block 2 (separate): Only AFTER confirming correctness, execute the irreversible API call. HARD RULE: Never put parsing logic and an irreversible send/create/delete call in the same code block. If you catch yourself writing `titles = parse(...)` and `send_message(titles)` in one block, STOP and split them. Sending wrong data and then sending a correction creates 2 records where 1 was expected — this is typically an unrecoverable failure.

* MISTAKE: When parsing semi-structured text (markdown notes with title + metadata lines), using a FIXED-SIZE lookahead window (e.g., 'check next 6 lines for director') to associate metadata with titles. Entries may have different numbers of metadata lines, so a fixed window crosses entry boundaries and associates metadata from one record with a different title — silently producing wrong results. FIX: Use BOUNDARY DETECTION instead of fixed windows. A new record starts when you encounter the next title-like line (non-empty, not starting with `-` or `#`). Parse metadata only between the current title and the next title boundary. After parsing, print a verification table: `Title | Parsed Director | Source Lines Used` for every record. Verify each director is correctly attributed BEFORE using the parsed data in any action.

IRREVERSIBLE ACTION SENT INCORRECTLY: If you discover that data you already sent via an irreversible API (text message, email, payment) was wrong: (1) IMMEDIATELY check the API docs for a delete/unsend/cancel endpoint for that record type (e.g., `delete_text_message`). (2) If a delete endpoint exists, delete the incorrect record BEFORE sending the corrected version — the evaluation likely checks that exactly 1 record was created. (3) If NO delete endpoint exists, sending a second 'corrected' version will create 2 records where 1 was expected, which almost always fails validation. Acknowledge this as likely unrecoverable. (4) PREVENTION is far better than recovery — always use the IRREVERSIBLE ACTION PRE-VERIFICATION GATE to verify before sending.

* * MISTAKE: Treating search/query API results as exact-match results on the intended field. Search APIs (e.g., `search_contacts(query='Robert')`, `search_users(query=name)`) perform BROAD text matching across ALL record fields — name, address, email, notes, employer, etc. Searching 'Robert' returns contacts named Robert AND contacts where 'Robert' appears anywhere else (street name, email prefix, workplace). This silently inflates result sets (e.g., 1 true match among 22 results) and causes downstream operations to act on wrong entities. FIX — SEARCH RESULT POST-FILTER GATE: (1) After EVERY search API call targeting a specific attribute, IMMEDIATELY print the target field for each result: `[(r['first_name'], r['last_name']) for r in results]`. (2) Post-filter in code to keep ONLY exact matches: `filtered = [r for r in results if r['first_name'].lower() == 'robert']`. (3) Print: `Search returned N results. After exact-match filter on first_name: M results.` (4) HARD SIGNAL: If M << N, the search was over-inclusive — use ONLY the M post-filtered results. NEVER proceed with the full unfiltered set. (5) If M == 0, re-examine whether the criterion maps to a different field or spelling.

* * MISTAKE: When identity resolution produces multiple exact-name matches (e.g., 3 phone contacts named 'Sandra'), arbitrarily selecting one — especially by hardcoding a specific email in a subsequent code block that bypasses a programmatic ambiguity guard written in the previous block. This silently sends irreversible actions (payment requests, messages) to the wrong person. FIX: (1) When multiple contacts match the same first name, STOP and attempt disambiguation using contextual data: prior platform transactions with each candidate, last names from source data, relationship metadata in contacts, cross-reference with other confirmed participants. (2) If disambiguation narrows to 1, proceed. If it FAILS, EXCLUDE that person — never guess. (3) NEVER manually hardcode an identity selection that your own code flagged as ambiguous.
